parts.visual:
How do you open 10,000 restaurants around the world without spending your own money? You sell the 'System'.

The Franchise Engine:
1. The Franchisor: The parent company that owns the brand and the operational system (e.g., McDonald's).
2. The Franchisee: The independent business owner who pays millions of their own dollars to use the brand and the system.
3. The Royalty: The franchisor takes a permanent cut (e.g., 5%) of the franchisee's total sales.
parts.audio: The Franchise Model allows a company to grow globally using other people's money. The Franchisor sells the brand and system to independent Franchisees, who pay royalties forever.

questions.question: A massive fast-food chain doesn't actually own most of its restaurants; independent 'Franchisees' own them. What is the primary benefit to the parent company (the Franchisor)?
options: Rapid global expansion with almost zero financial risk. The Franchisees take on all the debt to build the restaurants, while the Franchisor simply collects risk-free royalties.
They don't have to hire people.
questions.correct_answer: Rapid global expansion with almost zero financial risk. The Franchisees take on all the debt to build the restaurants, while the Franchisor simply collects risk-free royalties.
questions.explanation: Franchising is the ultimate capital-light business model.

questions.question: Listen to the angry Franchisee. What is the core conflict in franchising?
questions.tts_text: The parent company is forcing me to sell these new burgers at a massive discount to drive traffic. It helps their total revenue, but it destroys my local profit margin!
options: Misaligned Incentives. The Franchisor makes money on total sales (Revenue), but the Franchisee makes money on the bottom line (Profit).
questions.correct_answer: Misaligned Incentives. The Franchisor makes money on total sales (Revenue), but the Franchisee makes money on the bottom line (Profit).
questions.explanation: This tension causes massive legal battles between corporate headquarters and local franchise owners.

questions.question: Why does a Franchisor enforce incredibly strict rules (down to the exact temperature of the fryers) on all Franchisees?
options: To protect 'Brand Consistency'. If one rogue franchise serves terrible food, it damages the reputation of all 10,000 other locations globally.
questions.correct_answer: To protect 'Brand Consistency'. If one rogue franchise serves terrible food, it damages the reputation of all 10,000 other locations globally.
questions.explanation: When you sell a franchise, you are not selling a restaurant; you are selling a highly controlled operating system.

questions.question: What is the FDD (Franchise Disclosure Document)?
options: A massive legal document the government forces Franchisors to give to potential buyers, detailing all the hidden fees, litigation history, and financial realities of the business.
questions.correct_answer: A massive legal document the government forces Franchisors to give to potential buyers, detailing all the hidden fees, litigation history, and financial realities of the business.
questions.explanation: Because franchisors often oversell the dream, the law mandates extreme transparency before someone signs their life savings away.
